title: The AI Backend Ecosystem
description: See where C# and .NET fit in the AI landscape, from local models to cloud APIs, and understand the main building blocks of an AI-powered backend.

blocks.text: AI is no longer limited to data science notebooks. Modern backends can classify text, answer questions over private data, automate workflows, and even reason about business rules. For .NET developers, this means new components: embedding models, vector databases, LLM clients, retrieval pipelines, and protocol servers like MCP.

blocks.title: What an AI backend usually combines
items: **LLM client** — calls a language model such as Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Ollama, or a local GGUF model.
**Embedding model** — converts text into numeric vectors so meaning can be compared and searched.
**Vector store** — persists embeddings and supports similarity search, often with metadata filtering.
**Retriever** — finds the most relevant pieces of context for a given question or task.
**Prompt composer** — assembles system instructions, retrieved context, and user input safely.
**Agent or planner** — decides which tools to call and how to combine their results.

cards.title: Microsoft.Extensions.AI
cards.description: A set of common abstractions for embeddings and LLMs from Microsoft, designed to work across providers.
pros: Supports OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, and Ollama
cons: Fewer production examples than older libraries

cards.title: Semantic Kernel
cards.description: An SDK for building AI agents, RAG pipelines, and plugin-based workflows in .NET.

cards.title: LLamaIndex.TS / .NET
cards.description: Data-framework focused on connecting LLMs to external data with indexing, retrieval, and agent modules.

cards.title: Model Context Protocol SDK
cards.description: Implementation of MCP for exposing backend tools and data to AI clients in a standardized way.

blocks.title: Local or cloud first?
blocks.text: You do not need a cloud account to start. Ollama and local GGUF models let you experiment privately. Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, and hosted embedding services become attractive once you need reliability, scale, or data governance.

terms.definition: A numeric vector that represents the meaning of text. Similar meanings produce similar vectors.
A database optimized for storing and searching high-dimensional vectors.
A basic unit of text for a language model, roughly a word or part of a word. LLMs charge and reason in tokens.
Retrieval-augmented generation: augmenting LLM prompts with relevant retrieved context.
Model Context Protocol: an open standard for exposing backend resources and tools to AI clients.

items.text: I can name at least three components of an AI backend
items.hint: Embedding model, vector store, LLM client, retriever, prompt composer, agent

items.text: I know when to choose local models versus cloud APIs
items.hint: Local for privacy and low cost; cloud for scale, governance, and managed reliability

items.text: I can match a library to a task
items.hint: Semantic Kernel for agents; Microsoft.Extensions.AI for provider abstraction; MCP for backend exposure

blocks.title: Lesson Summary
points: AI backends combine LLM clients, embeddings, vector stores, retrievers, and agents.
.NET has mature libraries for each layer, including Microsoft.Extensions.AI, Semantic Kernel, and MCP SDKs.
Start with local tools, then adopt cloud services when you need governance or scale.
blocks.takeaway: Think in layers: retrieval, generation, tools, and orchestration. Each layer has a purpose, and .NET has a library for it.
